A FIELD GUIDE TO YOUR LITTLE TROUBLEMAKER

Pride.

When confidence wants an audience.

You care about doing things well — and, occasionally, about everyone noticing. Your inner headliner brings confidence, high standards, and a small imaginary spotlight.

IN THIS GUIDE

The meaningEveryday momentsA useful distinctionReading your scoreA little balanceGood questions

A character to get curious about.
Not a label to live inside.

THE SHORT VERSION

What does pride mean?

In our quiz, pride is the pull to protect an impressive image of yourself. Doing good work matters, but being seen doing good work can start to matter just as much. The little troublemaker appears when recognition feels necessary, or a correction feels like a threat to your whole identity.

The good energy

You step up, take ownership, and give your best work a little extra polish.

The little tripwire

Being seen as capable can make asking for help or admitting a mistake feel unusually difficult.

SUSPICIOUSLY FAMILIAR?

Little moments.
Recognizable habits.

These are illustrations, not extra test questions. One familiar moment does not define you.

The shared success

A project goes well. Before enjoying the outcome, you scan the thank-you message to see whether your contribution made the list.

The helpful suggestion

Someone offers a simpler approach. You spend the next few minutes explaining why your original plan was reasonable, even though you would rather use theirs.

The small correction

You know you mixed up a detail, but admitting it in front of the group feels much bigger than the mistake itself.

ROOM FOR NUANCE

Pride and confidence

Confidence can make room for “I don’t know yet.” The pattern explored here is the urge to keep looking capable, even when asking a question or sharing credit would help. Enjoying an achievement does not automatically fit that pattern.

IF THIS CHARACTER SHOWED UP IN YOUR RESULT

Read the score.
Keep the context.

A higher pride score

A higher pride score means you more often endorsed our statements about recognition and difficulty accepting correction. Look for the situations where you feel a need to defend your image. It does not measure your worth, leadership ability, or narcissism.

A lower pride score

A lower score means those particular statements fit less closely. It does not mean you lack confidence or ambition; you may simply relate differently to attention and feedback.

How the number works

Each tendency has three equally weighted questions, answered from 0 to 4. Balancing statements are reverse-scored. The total out of 12 is converted to a rounded score out of 100. Your seven scores are independent; they do not add up to 100. A tie stays a tie.

A score is not a population percentile, a diagnosis, or a fixed personality type. Read the scoring explanation.

A SMALL EXPERIMENT

A little more humility.

In your next conversation, ask one sincere question about another person’s idea. Listen long enough to summarize it before explaining your own. The aim is curiosity, not making yourself smaller.

Three questions to sit with

  • When did I last want credit more than I wanted progress?
  • What might I learn if I did not have to look like the expert?
  • Who helped with something I recently called my achievement?

No perfect answer required. Pick the question that feels useful and leave the rest.

BEFORE YOU MAKE IT YOUR WHOLE PERSONALITY

Good questions.

Is feeling proud of my work a bad thing?

No. Satisfaction in effort and progress is different from needing to feel superior. This character is a playful way to examine how you respond to recognition and correction.

Does a high pride score mean I am a narcissist?

No. Three entertainment questions cannot establish a clinical condition or a fixed personality type. Read the individual situations rather than turning the score into a diagnosis.
